question: Write the Python statement that imports the standard-library module named math.
correct: import math
feedback: import math makes the math module's functions and values available, accessed as math.something.

question: A program runs  from math import sqrt  at the top, and later a line calls  math.sqrt(9). What happens?
correct: A NameError, because only sqrt was brought in, not the name math
incorrect: It works, since from-import also makes the module's own name available
A SyntaxError, because from-import may not be used on a function name
It works, because Python looks up any missing name in the library
feedback: from-import binds just the names you list. Either import the module and use math.sqrt, or import sqrt and call it bare — mixing the two forms is what fails.

question: Arrange these lines into a working program that prints the area of a circle of radius 3, rounded to two decimal places.
feedback: The import has to come before any use of math.pi, and the dotted name is how you reach inside the module. Each later line depends on a name the line above it created.

question: In the expression  math.pi, what does the  math  part tell you?
correct: That pi lives inside the math namespace
incorrect: That pi is a method you must call with parentheses
That pi is a variable you defined in your own file
That math is the name of your current program
feedback: A namespace answers 'where does this name live?' math.pi means the name pi is found inside the math module's namespace.

question: tools.py sits in the same folder as main.py and defines  def area(w, h). Which line in main.py makes  tools.area(2, 3)  work?
correct: import tools
incorrect: import tools.py
from tools import area
import area from tools
feedback: Your own file is a module just like math: import it by its name without the .py, and reach what it defines through the dot. from tools import area would bring in area alone — the name tools would not exist, so tools.area(2, 3) would fail.

question:
{{1}} random
roll = random.{{2}}(1, 6)
print(roll)

Complete the program so that it prints a whole number from 1 to 6, like a die.
feedback: import random makes the module's name available, and everything inside it is then reached through the dot. randint(1, 6) includes BOTH ends, which is what a die needs.

question: After  import math, what number does  math.floor({{a}} / {{b}})  produce?
feedback_template: {{a}} / {{b}} is a float, and floor drops down to the nearest whole number below it, giving {{expected}} rather than a rounded result.

question: NPC: One mould, many golems
intro: Zoya lifts a wooden mould from the shelf and sets it beside a row of clay figures. “People mix these two up constantly,” they say. “The mould is the class. The figures are the objects. Let me show you in code.”

beats.say: This is a class. It is the mould: a description of what every golem will have. Writing it builds no golem at all.
Nothing exists yet. A class is only the blueprint.

steps.say:
Calling the class is what presses a figure out of the mould. Each call builds a new object, also called an instance.
ash = Golem("Ash")
birch = Golem("Birch")
Two calls, so two objects. Each one carries its own name attribute.

beats.say: Calling the class is what presses a figure out of the mould. Each call builds a new object, also called an instance.
Two calls, so two objects. Each one carries its own name attribute.

check.prompt: How many Golem objects exist after those two lines?
check.answer: Two — each call to Golem() builds a new object
wrong: One — ash and birch are two names for it
check.why: Every call to the class builds a fresh object. Two names for ONE object would need ash = birch, which is not what was written.

steps.say: So count them separately: one class, written once, and as many objects as there were calls. Change ash.name and birch.name stays as it was.

beats.say: So count them separately: one class, written once, and as many objects as there were calls. Change ash.name and birch.name stays as it was.

outro: Zoya sets the mould down. “One blueprint, many objects. Now you count some.”

question: A program defines  class Dog:  once, and later runs  rex = Dog()  and  fido = Dog(). How many classes and objects now exist?
correct: One class, and two objects built from it
incorrect: Two classes, one made by each call to Dog()
One class and one object, shared by two names
One object, since rex and fido are both Dog
feedback: A class is the blueprint; an object (or instance) is one thing built from it. Each call to Dog() builds a NEW object, so rex and fido are two separate objects of the one class — unlike  fido = rex, which would give one object two names.

question: Two objects each hold their own data. What does this program print?
code:
class Citizen:
    def __init__(self, name, balance):
        self.name = name
        self.balance = balance

elaine = Citizen("Elaine", 120)
percival = Citizen("Percival", 40)
elaine.balance = elaine.balance + 50
print(percival.balance)
feedback: Each object gets its own copy of the data set up in __init__, so changing elaine's balance leaves percival's alone. The class is shared; the instance data is not.

question: Write the Python header line that begins the definition of a class named Dog. (Just the header, no body.)
correct: class Dog:
feedback: A class definition starts with the keyword class, the name, and a colon: class Dog:

question: Write the Python header line that begins the definition of a class named B whose parent class is A. (Just the header, no body.)
correct: class B(A):
feedback: The parent goes in parentheses after the new class's name, which is how Python knows to look in A for anything B does not define itself.

question: NPC: The word that makes a change stick
intro: A row of half-finished clay golems lines Zoya's workbench. They tap one on the shoulder. “Each of these is one object — one thing built from a class. Every method you write is handed the particular object it is working on, and the name for that is self. Forgetting it is the quietest bug in this wing.”

beats.say: Here is a class for a tally. Every golem I build from it is one Tally object:
self.n = 0 writes the number onto this object, and it stays there after __init__ ends. A value kept on an object like that is called an attribute.

steps.say:
Now a method that means to count up, but slips:
    def bump(self):
        n = self.n + 1
It reads self.n correctly and adds one. But it stores the result in a plain n. That is a local variable — a scratch note on the bench rather than a mark on the golem — and it is thrown away the moment the method ends.

check.prompt: After calling bump() once on a fresh Tally, what is self.n?
check.answer: Still 0 — the update went to a scratch variable
wrong: The program crashes on the missing attribute
check.why: The arithmetic was right, but nothing was written back to the object. n was a local variable, so it was swept away with the bench notes when the method ended, and the attribute self.n was never touched.

beats.say: Now a method that means to count up, but slips:

It reads self.n correctly and adds one. But it stores the result in a plain n. That is a local variable — a scratch note on the bench rather than a mark on the golem — and it is thrown away the moment the method ends.

steps.say: The fix is one word on the LEFT of the equals sign: self.n = self.n + 1. Reading needs self. too, but the left side is what decides whether the change lands on the object or on a scratch note that is about to be thrown away.

outro: “The next question shows you this exact slip. You already know where the change went.”

correct: Without self. it creates a local variable that soon disappears
incorrect: The subtraction happens before the assignment, so the old value is used
A method is unable to change data that __init__ created
The method is missing a return statement at the end
feedback: Bare balance is a throwaway local name. The fix is one word: self.balance = self.balance - amount. When an update mysteriously does not stick, check for a missing self. first.

feedback_template: __init__ starts this object's n at {{start}}, and each bump() adds {{step}} to it. Because the update is written to self.n, it persists between calls: {{calls}} calls leave {{expected}}.

question:
class Citizen:
    def __init__(self, name, balance):
        self.name = name
        self.balance = balance
    def pay(self, amount):
        self.balance = self.balance - amount

elaine = Citizen("Elaine", 120)
percival = Citizen("Percival", 40)
elaine.pay(30)
percival.pay(5)
elaine.pay(10)

After this runs, elaine.balance is {{1}} and percival.balance is {{2}}.
feedback: pay() is written once, but self is whichever object it was called on. elaine.pay(...) touches only Elaine's balance (120 - 30 - 10 = 80), and percival.pay(5) only Percival's (40 - 5 = 35). Same class, separate data.

question:
These are lines {{l0}} to {{l7}} of a larger file. The program prints 0 where 5 was expected. Type the number of the ONE line that has to change.

{{l0}}  class Purse:
{{l1}}      def __init__(self):
{{l2}}          self.coins = 0
{{l3}}      def add(self, n):
{{l4}}          coins = self.coins + n
{{l5}}  p = Purse()
{{l6}}  p.add(5)
{{l7}}  print(p.coins)
feedback_template: Line {{expected}} computes the right number and then stores it in a plain coins — a local variable that vanishes when add() returns. It needs to say self.coins = self.coins + n. Every other line is fine, which is what makes this bug so quiet: nothing crashes, the purse just never fills.

question: The special setup method that runs automatically when an object is created is named ___.
correct: __init__
feedback: __init__ (two underscores on each side) initializes a new object's attributes when it is created.

prompt: Fill in the blanks so this class stores the fuel it is given and prints 5.
feedback: The setup method runs automatically when you call the class like a function. Assigning to self.fuel is what makes the value stick to this particular object — a bare fuel = fuel would set a local variable that vanishes when the method returns.

question: Inside a method, write the Python statement that stores the parameter  n  onto the object as an attribute called n.
correct: self.n = n
feedback: self.name = name puts the value on the object, so it travels with that object. Leaving off self. would create a local variable that vanishes.

question: Arrange what Python does, in order, when you write dog = Dog("Rex").
items: Create a new, empty object of the class
Call __init__, passing the new object in as self
Store "Rex" onto self as an attribute
Hand the finished object back to be named dog
feedback: Construction is object-first: Python builds the empty object, calls __init__ with it as self, the body of __init__ attaches the starting attributes, and only then is the finished object handed back to your variable.

question: NPC: Standing on the parent's shoulders
intro: Zoya is fitting a helmet onto a golem that already has arms and legs. “I did not sculpt those again,” they say. “A child class starts from everything its parent class already does. That is inheritance, and super() is how the child asks the parent to do its part.”

beats.say: Here is a parent class. Its __init__ stores one attribute.
A child class names its parent in parentheses. Inside the child's __init__, super().__init__(name) runs the parent's setup, so self.name gets stored without being retyped.
After that line, the child adds what only a Sentinel has.

check.prompt: Which line is responsible for a Sentinel having a name attribute?
wrong: class Sentinel(Golem):, which copies every attribute across
self.shield = 3, which creates all the attributes
check.why: Naming the parent gives the child its METHODS. Attributes are created only when an __init__ actually runs — and super() is what runs the parent's.

steps.say: Once super() has run, the child may use or change what the parent set up: self.shield = self.shield + 1 would work, and so would anything that reads self.name.

beats.say: Once super() has run, the child may use or change what the parent set up: self.shield = self.shield + 1 would work, and so would anything that reads self.name.

outro: Zoya taps the helmet. “Parent first, then the child's own additions. Trace one yourself.”

question: A child class calls super() and then adjusts what it inherited. What does this program print?
feedback: super().__init__(8) sets self.legs to 8 first; the next line reads that attribute back and stores 2 more onto the same object.

question: Arrange these lines into a working class and program: a Lantern that starts with a fuel level, burns one unit, and then reports what is left.
feedback: The whole class body is indented under the header, and each method header sits at the same level as the others. Nothing outside the class can run until the class exists, so the three unindented lines come last, in the order create, act, report.

question: A function defined inside a class, which acts on that object's own data, is called a ___.
correct: method
feedback: A method is just a function that lives inside a class and takes self as its first parameter.

question: Why does a leading underscore, as in  self._pin, matter in Python?
correct: It is a convention marking the value internal, not a real lock
incorrect: It makes Python refuse any access from outside the class
It hides the attribute from dir() and from the object's __dict__
It turns the attribute read-only, so assignment to it fails
feedback: Python has no hard privacy. The underscore is a message to humans: reach this through a method such as check_pin() rather than touching it directly. That discipline is encapsulation.

question: What is an attribute, as opposed to a method?
correct: A piece of data stored on an object, such as self.name
incorrect: A function defined inside a class, such as speak(self)
The first parameter of every method, written as self
A value passed into __init__ but not stored on the object
feedback: An attribute is data that belongs to an object. You set it with self.name = ... and read it back with object.name.

question: A class defines  def speak(self):, yet code outside calls  dog.speak()  and passes no arguments at all. Why is that not an error?
correct: Calling through the object hands that object in as self automatically
incorrect: self holds a default value that the class body quietly supplies
self is optional, so Python drops it when no argument is given
Python skips the first parameter of any function defined in a class
feedback: dog.speak() is shorthand for handing dog to the method as its first argument, which is why self is written in the definition but not at the call.

question: This class defines __str__. What does the program print?
correct: Ayla (9)
feedback: print() asks the object for its text form, and __str__ is the method that supplies it. Without __str__ you would see something like <__main__.Hero object at 0x...>: the object works either way, it just describes itself badly.

question: What does the line  class Knight(Guard):  mean?
correct: Knight inherits Guard's attributes and methods, and can add more
incorrect: Knight stores a Guard object inside each knight
Knight and Guard are two names for the very same class
Guard is passed as an argument each time a new Knight object is built
feedback: The parentheses mark inheritance: Guard is the parent, Knight is the child. Even an empty Knight body already has everything Guard defined.

prompt: Fill in the blanks so Wolf inherits from Animal, overrides the greeting, and prints  howl.
feedback: The parent class goes in the parentheses of the class header. Defining a method with the same name in the child overrides the inherited one, so Python finds the child version first and the parent version is never reached.

question: Guard is already defined, and its __init__(self, name) stores self.name. Arrange these lines into a child class and a program that prints Sir Lia.
feedback: super().__init__(name) runs the parent's setup, which is what creates self.name. The title line reads self.name, so it has to come AFTER the super() call: until the parent's __init__ has run, the attribute does not exist yet.

question: In  class Knight(Guard):, Guard is the {{1}} class and Knight is the {{2}} class; inside Knight's own __init__, the call {{3}}().__init__(name) runs Guard's setup so it need not be retyped.
feedback: The name in the parentheses of the class header is the one being inherited from, and super() is the standard way for the new class to reach it without naming it twice.

correct: Sir Lancelot leads the patrol.
incorrect: Lancelot is on patrol.
An error, because Knight has no __init__
Sir Lancelot is on patrol.
feedback: Knight inherits __init__ from Guard, so the name is stored. Knight also defines its own patrol, which overrides the parent's version for knight objects.

question: A Knight class overrides patrol() but defines no __init__ of its own. What happens when Knight("Lancelot") is created?
correct: The parent's __init__ runs, so the object still gets its name attribute
incorrect: Python raises an error, because every class needs its own __init__
The object is built with no attributes at all until one is assigned
Knight's patrol() runs first so the object has something to work with
feedback: A child that defines no __init__ simply inherits the parent's. Overriding one method has no effect on the others — Knight replaces patrol() and keeps everything else.

feedback_template: Rider has no __init__, so Beast's runs and stores legs = {{legs}}. Rider DOES override feet(): it asks the parent's version for {{legs}} through super(), then adds {{extra}}, giving {{expected}}.

question: Defining a method in a child class with the same name as the parent's, so the child's version wins, is called an ___.
correct: override
feedback: Overriding lets a child specialize one behavior while keeping everything else it inherited.

question: One loop calls the same method on a mix of objects. What does the program print?
correct:
hi
ho
hi
feedback: The loop never checks a type. Each object looks for cry() in its OWN class first, so the Knight in the middle answers "ho" while the Guards answer "hi". One call, the right behaviour for each object: that is polymorphism.

question: A list holds a mix of Guard and Knight objects, and a loop calls  officer.patrol()  on each without checking their types. Which idea makes this work?
correct: Polymorphism — each object runs the version from its own class
incorrect: Encapsulation — the objects hide their data from the loop
Composition — the list contains the objects rather than inheriting them
Abstraction — the loop is written at a higher level than the objects
feedback: One method name, many behaviors, chosen automatically by the object. Add a new kind of officer tomorrow and this loop keeps working untouched — no if-statement to update.

question: You are deciding between inheritance and composition. Which of these are best modelled as "is-a" relationships, suited to inheritance? (Select all that apply)
correct: A Knight and a Guard
A LeadResearcher and a Researcher
incorrect: A Squad and the guards it contains
A Study and its list of participants
A DispatchDesk and the packages waiting on it
feedback: A knight is a kind of guard, so inheritance fits. A squad is not a kind of guard — it has guards, which is composition. When one thing merely contains another, store it rather than inherit from it.

question: A BankAccount keeps its total in  self._balance  and changes it only inside deposit() and withdraw(), which both reject negative amounts. What does that design actually buy?
correct: Every change to the balance runs through code that can enforce the rules
incorrect: The balance becomes genuinely unreachable from outside the class in Python
The class no longer needs an __init__, since the methods set the balance
Each account ends up sharing one balance, keeping the bank's totals in step
feedback: This is encapsulation doing its job: the value and the rules that protect it live together, so no caller can put the object into a state it should never be in.

question: An Account object starts with self.balance = {{start}}. It calls deposit({{dep}}) once and then withdraw({{wd}}) once. What is self.balance afterward?
feedback_template: Deposit adds and withdraw subtracts from the object's own balance: {{start}} + {{dep}} - {{wd}} = {{expected}}.

question: Why is  members = []  written directly in a class body a bug when each object should have its own list?
correct: One list is shared by every object, so adding shows up in all
incorrect: Each object gets its own copy, but the copies cannot be appended to
The list belongs to the class, so no object can read it through self
The list is rebuilt empty each time a new object is created
feedback: Anything that should differ between objects belongs in __init__ as self.members = []. This is the OOP cousin of the aliasing trap: one object, many names pointing at it.

question: members is written in the class body, not in __init__. What does the program print?
code:
class Squad:
    members = []
    def add(self, who):
        self.members.append(who)

a = Squad()
b = Squad()
a.add("Lia")
b.add("Oz")
print(len(a.members))
feedback: There is only ONE list, stored on the class, and both squads reach it through self.members. Oz was added through b, yet shows up in a. Writing self.members = [] inside __init__ gives every squad a list of its own, and the answer would be 1.

question: Which of the following are true about the 'forgot self.' and 'shared mutable class attribute' bugs? (Select all that apply)
correct: Forgetting self. makes an update disappear when the method ends
A mutable class attribute is shared across every object
Putting self.items = [] in __init__ gives each object its own list
incorrect: Both bugs cause Python to refuse to start the program
Both bugs only appear in classes that use inheritance
feedback: Forgetting self. loses the change to a local variable; a class-body list is shared by all instances. Creating the list in __init__ fixes the sharing. Neither bug stops the program from running.

question:
These are lines {{l0}} to {{l5}} of a larger file. Every squad turns out to share the same recruits. Type the number of the line that causes it.

{{l0}}  class Squad:
{{l1}}      members = []
{{l2}}      def __init__(self, name):
{{l3}}          self.name = name
{{l4}}      def recruit(self, who):
{{l5}}          self.members.append(who)
feedback_template: Line {{expected}} creates the list in the class body, so it is made once and belongs to the class: every Squad reaches that same list through self.members. The cure is to delete it and write self.members = [] inside __init__, which runs once per object. The append line is innocent — it does exactly what it says.
count lives on the class, not on any one object, so every construction adds {{step}} to the same shared number: {{n}} objects bring it to {{expected}}.

question: What is abstraction in the context of OOP and computer science?
correct: Hiding complicated details behind a simple surface
incorrect: Bundling data together with the methods that change it
Giving one method name a different body in each class
Building a new class on top of an existing parent class
feedback: Abstraction lets you use something through a simple interface without knowing its inner workings, like driving a car without understanding the engine.

question: Using the noun/verb heuristic on a problem description, what do the nouns and verbs suggest?
correct: Nouns suggest classes and attributes; verbs suggest methods
incorrect: Nouns suggest methods; verbs suggest classes and attributes
Nouns suggest modules; verbs suggest the imports they need
Nouns suggest parameters; verbs suggest their default values
feedback: Write the problem in plain English, then underline. 'A courier picks up a package' gives classes Courier and Package, and a method pick_up. It will not hand you a perfect design, but it gets you off the blank page.

question: Match each pillar of object-oriented programming to the situation that shows it.

pairs.definition: A balance that changes only through deposit() and withdraw()
Calling sorted() with no idea how it sorts
class Knight(Guard): getting patrol() without retyping it
One loop calling speak() on a mix of Wolf and Owl objects

feedback: Encapsulation guards data behind methods. Abstraction lets you use something without knowing its insides. Inheritance reuses a parent's code in a child. Polymorphism lets one call do the right thing for each kind of object.

question: A class tracks packages, couriers, billing, and the weather. Which design idea does it violate?
correct: Cohesion — a class should have one clear responsibility
incorrect: Coupling — a class should not talk to any other class
Inheritance — a class ought to extend some parent class
Encapsulation — a class should hold at most one attribute
feedback: That class has low cohesion: four unrelated jobs in one box. The design goal is high cohesion (each class minds one job) and low coupling (changing one class does not force rewrites elsewhere).

correct: Report.send breaks too: Report depends on Mailer's insides
incorrect: Nothing: an attribute is private to the class defining it
Only Mailer changes: a rename cannot reach another class
Python updates the old name wherever it has been used
feedback: Report reaches into Mailer and sets its attributes directly, so the two are tightly coupled: a change inside one forces a change in the other. Had Report called a method such as mailer.deliver(text) and nothing else, Mailer could rename whatever it liked. Python has no private attributes and renames nothing for you.

question: A Report class is split so that gathering the data, formatting it, and emailing it each live in their own class. Which pair of qualities does that improve?
correct: Higher cohesion within each class, and looser coupling between them
incorrect: Higher cohesion, at the cost of tighter coupling between the pieces
Looser coupling, at the cost of lower cohesion inside each piece
Neither, since splitting a class only moves the same code around
feedback: Each class now does one job (cohesion), and each depends on less of the others (coupling). The two usually improve together when a responsibility is separated cleanly.

question: Match each relationship to the line of Python that expresses it.

pairs.term: A Knight is a kind of Guard
A Wolf speaks in its own way

feedback: "Is a kind of" is inheritance: the parent goes in the parentheses. "Has" is composition: the other object, or a list of them, is stored as an attribute. Prefer composition whenever one thing merely contains another — a Squad is not a kind of Guard. Behaving in its own way is an override, which needs no new relationship at all.

question: Building an object out of other objects, a "has-a" relationship rather than an "is-a" one, is called ___.
correct: composition
feedback: A famous guideline says to favour composition over inheritance: you can change what an object contains while the program runs, but you cannot change a class's parent.

question: The course describes a tower of abstraction layers. Which ordering matches it, from lowest to highest?
correct: Transistors, logic gates, machine code, Python, your classes
incorrect: Python, machine code, logic gates, transistors, your classes
Your classes, Python, transistors, logic gates, machine code
Logic gates, transistors, Python, machine code, your classes
feedback: Each layer hides the mess below it. That is how a small mind builds a large machine: you write a class without ever thinking about transistors.

question: Match each object-oriented design term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: How focused a class is on one responsibility
How dependent classes are on one another
Building an object out of other objects
Replacing a parent's method in a child class

feedback: Good design aims for high cohesion and low coupling, uses composition for 'has-a' links, and overrides methods to specialize behavior.

question: What does this program print after two recruits?
feedback: Because self.members is created inside __init__, this squad has its own list. Two recruits were appended, so its length is 2.

question: A small Stack class wraps a list. What does this program print?
feedback: The class is an abstract data type: callers see only push() and pop(), and the list behind them is a detail. After push 1, push 2, pop (removing 2) and push 3, the newest item is 3, so that is what pop() returns.

question: A Deck object holds a list of {{n}} Card objects, and each Card stores  self.value = {{v}}. The deck's total() method adds up the value of every card it holds. What does total() return?
feedback_template: This is composition: the deck has cards rather than being one. Summing {{n}} cards worth {{v}} each gives {{expected}}.

question: NPC: Writing a method yourself
intro: Zoya clears a space on the bench and slides a slate across. “You have read enough classes,” they say. “Now you write them. The class is given; you supply one method. Two habits will carry you through.”

beats.say: First habit: anything the object must REMEMBER is written through self.
self.fuel is an attribute: it is still there after __init__ ends. A plain fuel would be gone.

steps.say:
Second habit: a method that changes the object reads the old value from self and stores the new one back on self.
    def burn(self):
        self.fuel = self.fuel - 1
Both sides say self.fuel. Leave it off the left side and the lamp never gets dimmer.

beats.say: Second habit: a method that changes the object reads the old value from self and stores the new one back on self.
Both sides say self.fuel. Leave it off the left side and the lamp never gets dimmer.

check.prompt: lamp = Lamp(3), then lamp.burn() twice. What is lamp.fuel?
check.answer: 1 — each call stored the smaller number back on the lamp
wrong: 3 — burn() works on a copy of the lamp
check.why: burn() writes to self.fuel, and self IS the lamp it was called on, so the change stays: 3, then 2, then 1.

steps.say: Your code is tested by building objects, calling your method, and then looking at what the object has become. Press Run as often as you like; it costs nothing.

beats.say: Your code is tested by building objects, calling your method, and then looking at what the object has become. Press Run as often as you like; it costs nothing.

outro: Zoya hands you the chalk. “Start small: teach a lantern to remember its fuel.”

question: Finish __init__ so that every new Lantern stores the fuel it was given in an attribute called fuel, and starts with an attribute called lit set to False.
hint: An attribute is made by assigning to it through self: self.fuel = fuel keeps the value on this lantern after __init__ ends.
feedback: __init__ runs once for each new object, and its job is to store what that object needs on self. fuel on its own is only a parameter, gone when __init__ returns; self.fuel is the attribute that stays.

question: Write add so that it puts n more coins in THIS purse. It does not need to return anything.
hint: Read the old amount from self.coins, and store the new amount back in self.coins. A plain coins would be a local variable.
feedback: The update has to be written to self.coins. coins = self.coins + n works out the right number and then drops it, because coins without self. is a local variable that vanishes when add() ends — the quietest bug in this chapter.

question: Write withdraw. If amount is more than the balance, change nothing and return False. Otherwise take amount off the balance and return True.
solution:
if amount > self.balance:
    return False
self.balance = self.balance - amount
return True
hint: Deal with the refusal first: if amount > self.balance, return False straight away. Whatever comes after that line only runs for a withdrawal that is allowed.
feedback: This is encapsulation doing its job: the balance changes only inside a method that checks the rule first, so no caller can overdraw the account by accident. Taking out exactly the balance is allowed, which is why the test is > and not >=.

question: Write __str__ so that printing a hero shows the name, then the hp in parentheses followed by " hp" — for example Ayla (9 hp).
hint: An f-string builds the text in one go: f"{self.name} (...)". __str__ must RETURN the text, not print it.
feedback: print(h) and str(h) both ask the object for its text by calling __str__, so it has to return a string. Reading self.name and self.hp at that moment is why the third test shows the hp after it changed.

question: A Squad keeps Guard objects in self.members. Write total_rank so that it returns the ranks of all its members added together — 0 for an empty squad.
solution:
total = 0
for guard in self.members:
    total = total + guard.rank
return total
hint: The accumulator pattern, over objects: start total at 0, loop over self.members, and add each guard.rank.
feedback: A squad HAS guards — composition — so the method walks the list the squad holds and reads each guard's own attribute. It is the same accumulator loop as in chapter 4; only what gets added has changed.

question: Write the whole class. A Stack starts empty. push(x) adds x on top; pop() removes the top item and returns it; size() returns how many items it holds. Every Stack must have its own items.

tests.run:
s = Stack()
s.push(1)
s.push(2)
s.pop()
s.push(3)

hint: Four methods, each beginning def ...(self...). Make the list in __init__ as self.items = [] so every stack gets its own; a list has append() and pop() already.
feedback: This is an abstract data type: callers see push, pop and size, and the list behind them is your business. The last test is the shared-list bug in disguise — write items = [] in the class body instead of self.items = [] in __init__ and every stack shares one list, so b would not be empty.
